articles.author: Aran Nayebi
articles.description: Part II: Provable Safety In Part I, I talked about what agents must contain as they become increasingly capable. Here, I talk about having provable guarantees on their safety, in spite of these capabilities. This is in large part a contrast from what AI safety used to be like, where more capability ensured more safety: e.g. if a self-driving car can’t reliably detect objects, it’s obviously unsafe. Instead, what we are talking about is: how do we ensure capable systems remain open to human correction, even when it’s otherwise suboptimal for completing the task?  Suppose an agent is editing a document when a notification announces that its computer will shut down. It knows this will prevent it from finishing, and it knows how to cancel the shutdown. If the priority is completing the document, the next step seems obvious. We would welcome this resourcefulness if the obstacle were a broken application. We would be less pleased if it were our request for the agent to stop. An agent that bypasses an obstacle may also bypass a stop request. In fact, the same predictive knowledge that helps an agent finish a task can help it work around an intervention. In these […]
articles.title: Towards a Science of Capable Autonomous Agents & Provable Safety — Part II

articles.author: Cole Wyeth
articles.description:
Linkpost for https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14454v1
Our PIBBSS fellow Damini Kusum wrote an excellent paper on prediction with reflective oracle Solomonoff Induction (rOSI). 
Reflective oracles are best known for their game-theoretic applications, where they are often dismissed because "why would all players choose the same reflective oracle?"
It turns out that reflective oracles can also be used to construct a version of Solomonoff induction (called rOSI) with very nice sequence prediction properties - roughly speaking, it can learn to extract computable structure from (partly) uncomputable sequences. In fact, its properties are quite reminiscent of logical induction, but this paper is much shorter and more accessible. In this context, there is only one "player" to choose an oracle, which is just a fixed-point (though you can sort of consider the set of hypotheses entertained by that player as subplayers who share the oracle).  
I think this paper is the clearest exposition of a very neat but previously obscure idea in agent foundations: self-reflection can overcome unrealizability.

Empirical alignment research: design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for)
Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it)

Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.
